meta.tagline: The birthplace of paella, a city shaped by oranges, and Spain's most underrated metropolis

pills: Eat paella at lunch, not dinner
Come in March for Las Fallas

overview.intro: Beach or history or architecture or food? Valencia is the city that doesn't make you choose. In a single day you can swim in the Mediterranean, get lost in medieval streets, find yourself surrounded by futuristic museums and sit down for lunch where the world's best paella was born. The Turia River running through the centre is the detail that completely changed Valencia's spirit: after the great flood of 1957, the riverbed was drained and turned into a 9-kilometre green park in the heart of the city. Today people cycle to work through it, run, spend time with their children here. Perhaps this is exactly what makes Valencia feel so good. Large but not exhausting, lively but not chaotic, and prices still feel reasonable compared to Spain's other big cities.

local_word.definition: The fertile farmland surrounding Valencia. Orange groves, rice paddies, chestnut fields. Valencian paella comes from these lands: chicken, rabbit, fresh beans, olive oil and bomba rice (a short-grain local rice that absorbs liquid well). No seafood — real Valencian paella is the food of agricultural land. Knowing this distinction means eating the right thing in the right place in the city.

rules.title: Paella is a lunch dish — not dinner
rules.description: Valencians eat paella at lunchtime, between 2pm and 4pm. Restaurants serving paella in the evening are generally tourist traps — they're almost certainly reheating paella cooked that morning. Real paella preparation starts in the morning and takes an average of 40-50 minutes to cook. If you want paella, plan your lunch around it and warn the group early.

rules.title: Don't drink orxata (horchata) from a supermarket
rules.description: Orxata is the city's drink — a sweet, creamy cold drink made from chufa (tiger nuts similar to tubers). It has nothing in common with the pasteurised supermarket version. For fresh orxata, look for a horchatería with 'orxata artesana' on the sign. Horchatería Santa Catalina near the Mercado Central is a historic spot and one of the best. Order a farton alongside — a long, lightly sweet roll made for dipping.

rules.title: Come in March for Las Fallas — but be ready for it
rules.description: Las Fallas (12-19 March) is Valencia's UNESCO-listed festival — enormous sculpture groups are erected across the city and burned on the final night. Hotels charge two to three times normal prices during this period and the city is packed. But seeing Valencia this way is only possible in March — never at any other time.

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct ideal · Jul–Aug hot · Dec–Feb mild

quick_facts.label: Food
quick_facts.value: Paella valenciana, orxata, agua de Valencia

tip.label: Cycling — the best way to see Valencia
tip.text: Valencia is a perfect city for cycling — flat and with excellent infrastructure. Valenbisi stations are everywhere — first 30 minutes free, then a nominal fee. Cycling along the Turia Gardens all the way down to the beach is Valencia's finest daily route. Rental bike alternatives are also widely available across the city.

overview.title: Welcome to Valencia

transport.intro: Valencia is small and flat. Cycling is the best option for getting around. For metro and bus, use the SUMA card system.

items.title: Airport → City
items.description: Metro Line 3 or Line 5 takes you from the airport to the city centre in about 20 minutes. Ticket €5.60 — airport surcharge included. Taxi to the centre around €20-25. Metro is easily the most practical option. SUMA card is valid on the airport line but the airport surcharge is paid separately.

items.title: Metro and tram
items.description: 5 metro lines and 4 tram lines under the Metrovalencia network. SUMA card (card itself €1.10) valid on all lines. Single fare approximately €1.50, 10-trip SUMA for Zone A €8.90. Runs from 5am to 1am, 24 hours on Friday and Saturday nights. The centre, Ruzafa, beach and City of Arts and Sciences are all reachable by metro or tram.

items.title: EMT Buses
items.description: Over 200 routes covering every corner of the city. Same SUMA card system applies. Cash payment on the bus is possible but slightly more expensive (€2). Night routes run after the metro closes. Bus is the most practical option for El Cabanyal and some coastal points.

items.title: Valenbisi — bike sharing
items.description: 275 stations and 2,750 bikes across the city. Annual subscription €25, daily €3.60. First 30 minutes free, hourly rate after that. Payment by contactless bank card at the station. Ideal for cycling along the Turia Gardens, to the beaches and around Ruzafa. The flat city makes it easy going.

items.title: Walking
items.description: Valencia's centre is small and walkable. From the Mercado Central: Cathedral 5 minutes, Turia Gardens entrance 10 minutes, Ruzafa 20 minutes. City of Arts and Sciences is 45 minutes on foot from the centre — long but a beautiful route through the Turia Gardens. Choose shaded routes on hot summer days.

callout.label: Valencia Tourist Card — is it worth it?
callout.text: 24 hours €15, 48 hours €20, 72 hours €25. Unlimited transport plus free entry to municipal museums. City of Arts and Sciences has a 15% discount — not fully free. Worth it if you're visiting several museums and moving around a lot. If you're only using the metro, the 10-trip SUMA card makes more sense.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Location matters in Valencia but the city is small enough that everywhere is easily accessible from everywhere.

local_word.definition: Valencia's liveliest and most creative neighbourhood. Its Arabic name means 'garden'. Ruzafa was an immigrant neighbourhood in the 1990s, transformed through the 2000s by artists, cafés and restaurants. Today it's packed with weekend markets, international restaurants, natural wine bars and art galleries. 20 minutes' walk from the city centre but a completely different character.

items.name: Ciutat Vella — historic centre
items.description: Cathedral, Mercado Central, La Lonja and El Carmen neighbourhood are all in this area. Walking distance to everything. Busy and touristy but the right place to experience Valencia's historic fabric. Staying in El Carmen means being close to nightlife — though equally close to morning noise.

items.name: Ruzafa (Russafa)
items.description: Creative neighbourhood — cafés, restaurants, bars and art galleries. Weekend Mercado de Ruzafa and an evening vermouth culture. 20 minutes on foot or 10 minutes to the metro. The best option for experiencing Valencia like a local.

items.name: El Cabanyal
items.description: 5 minutes' walk to the beach. Former fishing neighbourhood, now home to artists and young families. Colourful azulejo-tiled houses, narrow streets. The neighbourhood was saved from demolition and is now a protected area. 20 minutes to the centre by tram.

items.name: Ensanche
items.description: Elegantly planned neighbourhood from the 19th century — wide boulevards, Modernist buildings, Mercado de Colón. Close to business, quiet but lively. Borders Ruzafa.

items.name: Near City of Arts and Sciences
items.description: Santiago Calatrava's futuristic structures — L'Hemisfèric, Museu de les Ciències, L'Oceanogràfic — are in this area. Staying here means you can see the buildings in their quiet early-morning state before the crowds arrive. 15 minutes to the centre by tram.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Valencia is sunny year-round but each season offers a different city.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Las Fallas and the city in bloom
items.description: March begins with Las Fallas — the city's biggest festival runs 12-19 March. April and May are festival-free but ideal: temperatures 18-24°C, the scent of orange blossom in the air, crowds below summer levels. Semana Santa brings religious processions in April. This period offers the chance to see Valencia both at its most festive and at its most peaceful.

callout.label: Las Fallas — 12-19 March
callout.text: On UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Over 700 enormous sculpture groups (fallas) are erected, then burned on the final night in La Cremà (19 March). Every day at 2pm: mascleta — a pyrotechnic show in Plaza del Ayuntamiento that shakes the whole city. Fire, music, costumes, street parties until 3am. Hotel prices triple but the experience is unmatched.

items.subtitle: Spring · Las Fallas, orange blossom scent, mild weather

items.label: Summer
items.name: Beach season and nightlife
items.description: July and August are hot but not as crowded as Barcelona. Beaches — La Malvarrosa and Les Arenes — quiet on weekdays, busy on weekends. Nightlife runs late: dinner at 10pm, bars open until 3am. Feria de Julio brings concerts across the city. Before 10am and after 7pm the heat becomes bearable.

callout.label: La Malvarrosa beach — how to get there
callout.text: Tram (Line 4 or 6) or bus from the city centre, 20-25 minutes. The beach is free, clean and a long stretch of coastline. Fresh seafood is available in the neighbouring El Cabanyal fishing neighbourhood. On weekdays at 9am the beach is nearly empty.

items.subtitle: Summer · 35°C, sea at its finest, long evenings

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Second best time
items.description: September and October are Valencia's most comfortable period. Summer crowds gone, temperatures still 20-25°C, swimming in the sea still possible. Orange harvest begins. 9 October is Valencia's Day of the Valencian Community — the official regional holiday celebrated since 1238, with processions, traditional costumes and flower offerings; an authentic local celebration even if not as large as Las Fallas. Rain increases from November but the city is quiet and prices are low.

callout.label: Mercado Central — best in autumn
callout.text: Valencia's historic market, 8,000 square metres, over 1,000 stalls. The Modernist glass and iron structure dates from 1928. Fresh fruit, vegetables, fish, meat, local cheese and charcuterie. Open every day except Sundays, 7:30am-3pm. Best hours are between 9am and 11am — stalls are full and crowds are still light.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Harvest season, mild weather, fewer crowds

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet and sunny
items.description: From December to February, Valencia is one of Spain's mildest cities — average 15-17°C, many sunny days. Christmas lights and markets bring the city to life. Museums are empty, restaurants accessible without reservations. Late February sees Las Fallas preparations begin — pyrotechnic materials at stalls, sculptures being built in workshops.

callout.label: Paella in Valencia in winter
callout.text: Winter is the best time to eat paella in Valencia — restaurants are quiet, chefs at their best. El Palmar village (on the shores of Albufera Lake, 20km from the city) is considered the true home of paella. Going to El Palmar for a weekday lunch is one of Valencians' favourite rituals. Reservation recommended.

items.subtitle: Winter · Spain's mildest winter at 15°C average

monthly_highlights.text: Las Fallas: giant cardboard monuments, a mascletà noise feast every noon, and on the final night, all of it burned — the week the city renews itself with fire.
Feria de Julio: concerts, the battle of flowers, and seaside summer nights.
La Tomatina: the world's biggest tomato fight in Buñol — 40 minutes by train, tickets in advance.
Nou d'Octubre: Valencia Day — marzipan gifts in the mocadorà tradition, parades in the streets.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: Eating the wrong paella in Valencia is very easy; eating the right one takes a little research. The city handles the rest by itself.

local_word.definition: The original Valencian paella consists of chicken, rabbit, fresh beans, tomatoes, olive oil, saffron and bomba rice — no seafood. Cooked in a wide, shallow two-handled iron pan (paellera) over a wood fire. Socarrat is critical: the lightly scorched layer of rice that forms on the bottom of the pan. Scraping it up with a wooden spoon and eating it is a pleasure in itself. No socarrat means the paella isn't finished.

items.name: Paella Valenciana
items.description: The city's most iconic dish and also its most adulterated. If there are 10 types of paella on the menu, a photo menu, or they're serving it in the evening — don't go in. Real paella is a lunch dish, cooked over wood fire, taking 40-50 minutes. La Pepica (on Malvarrosa beach, since 1898) or restaurants in El Palmar village are the most reliable options. €15-25 per person.
items.tag: La Pepica, beach · El Palmar village · lunchtime · €15–25

items.name: Orxata con fartons
items.description: A sweet, cold drink made from chufa (tiger nuts). No milk, gluten-free and vegan. Alongside it, a farton — a long, lightly sweet roll made specifically for dipping into it. Between 5pm and 7pm, Valencians sit down for this pair. Try Horchatería Santa Catalina or anywhere with an 'orxata artesana' sign. Stay well away from the pasteurised supermarket version.
items.tag: Horchatería Santa Catalina · look for orxata artesana · afternoon

items.name: Agua de Valencia
items.description: Fresh orange juice, cava (Spanish sparkling wine), vodka or gin, sugar — Valencia's cocktail, served in a large jug. Invented in 1959 at Café Madrid. The real version made with fresh orange juice is completely different from the tourist version made with concentrate. The price tells you: €8-12 per jug.
items.tag: Café Madrid (original) · order by the jug · €8–12

items.name: Tapas — in El Cabanyal
items.description: El Cabanyal is Valencia's former fishing neighbourhood — the freshest seafood in the city comes from here. Clóchinas (Valencia's own small, intensely flavoured mussels, May-August season), coquilles (scallops) and pulpo (octopus) are the classics here. Bar Casa Montaña has been open since 1836 — small plates €3-5, excellent wine selection.
items.tag: El Cabanyal neighbourhood · Casa Montaña since 1836 · €3–5 per plate

items.name: Buñuelo
items.description: Deep-fried dough ball — crispy on the outside, soft inside. The sweet version is served with icing sugar. €1-2 at stalls inside Mercado Central or on the street. A breakfast or mid-morning snack. Found everywhere during Las Fallas.

items.name: Arroz al horno
items.description: Paella's sibling but very different: rice baked in the oven with chickpeas, aubergine, tomatoes, sausage and pork ribs, served in a clay pot. A winter dish — October to March. It lives in paella's shadow but is every bit as delicious.
items.tag: Local restaurants and home-style eateries · winter months · €12–18

callout.label: Vermouth hour — 12pm to 2pm
callout.text: Valencians drink vermouth before lunch — this isn't just a drink, it's the finest pause in the day. Ruzafa's bars are the heart of this ritual: tables outside, sunshine, olives and crisps alongside, conversations that stretch on. Bar Anaconda or Bar Cañas y Barro are ideal starting points for this experience.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Valencia's best corners are usually two streets away or just outside the city.

items.name: Estación del Norte
items.description: A Modernist train station built in 1917 — one of Valencia's most important architectural buildings, yet most visitors walk past without going inside. Stained glass windows, ceramic panels and ironwork decorated with orange blossom, orange trees and Valencian symbols. Valencia's agricultural culture is embedded in this building's walls. Go inside even if you're not catching a train.
items.rarity: Tourists constantly walk past Spain's most beautiful train station

items.name: Jardines del Turia
items.description: After the 1957 flood disaster, the Turia riverbed was drained and turned into a 9-kilometre green corridor running right through the heart of the city. Cycling paths, walking trails, playgrounds and Gulliver Park all along this corridor. Valencians run here, cycle, have picnics. Completely free.
items.rarity: Turia Gardens — former riverbed, now a 9km park

items.name: Albufera Lake
items.description: 20 kilometres south of Valencia, a freshwater lake separated from the Mediterranean by natural sand barriers. A 21,000-hectare natural park. El Palmar village sits in the middle of the lake and can be explored by wooden boat. At sunset the lake turns red — a spectacular sight. Just 40 minutes by bus from the city centre.
items.rarity: Albufera Lake — the true home of paella and a flamingo paradise

items.name: El Carmen neighbourhood
items.description: Narrow streets enclosed by medieval walls inside Ciutat Vella. Artist studios, alternative cafés and street art by day; bars and live music venues by night. Torres de Serranos offers one of the city's finest panoramas — free. Quietest in the early morning hours; nightlife peaks on Friday and Saturday.
items.rarity: El Carmen — a medieval neighbourhood still alive at midnight

items.name: La Lonja de la Seda (Silk Exchange)
items.description: Built between 1482 and 1548, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. One of Spain's finest examples of late Gothic architecture. The spiral columns and vaulted ceiling of the Salon de Contratación tell the story of Valencia's golden age of trade. 3 minutes' walk from the Mercado Central, with a fraction of the crowds.
items.rarity: La Lonja de la Seda — UNESCO's greatest gift to Valencia

items.name: Bioparc Valencia
items.description: At the western end of the Turia Gardens. Not a traditional caged zoo — all animals are in open areas that replicate their natural habitats, at the same observation level as visitors. Gorillas, chimpanzees, elephants and hippos observed this way is a different experience altogether. Valencia's finest activity for children, though adults are equally captivated.
items.rarity: Bioparc — not a zoo, but a window onto the African savannah

callout.label: Benimaclet — student neighbourhood and weekly market
callout.text: University neighbourhood in the north of the city, 15 minutes from the centre by metro. On Tuesdays a weekly market sets up — locally produced vegetables, fruit, cheese and pulses. Prices are half those of the Mercado Central. Not touristy, but the city's daily rhythm is visible here in its most authentic form.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Eat paella at lunch — in the right place
items.sub: Between 2pm and 4pm. La Pepica (beach, since 1898) or El Palmar village. No paella in the evening. Don't forget to ask for socarrat — that lightly scorched layer of rice on the bottom of the pan.

items.label: Drink orxata con fartons
items.sub: Horchatería Santa Catalina, near Mercado Central. Look for the 'orxata artesana' sign. Ideal between 5pm and 7pm in the afternoon.

items.label: Go to Mercado Central — early in the morning
items.sub: Open every day except Sundays, 7:30am-3pm. Best time 9-11am. Modernist building from 1928, over 1,000 stalls.

items.label: Cycle through Turia Gardens
items.sub: First 30 minutes free with Valenbisi. 9km route from the city centre all the way to the beach.

items.label: Visit La Lonja de la Seda
items.sub: 3 minutes from Mercado Central. UNESCO World Heritage Site. Low crowds. Don't miss going inside.

items.label: Visit Estación del Norte
items.sub: Modernist train station from 1917. Go inside for the stained glass and ceramics. No need to catch a train.

items.label: Drink vermouth in Ruzafa
items.sub: 12pm-2pm. Bar Anaconda or the bars around it. Small tapas come alongside. Sunday market at Mercado de Ruzafa.

items.label: Take an evening walk in El Carmen
items.sub: City panorama from Torres de Serranos — free. Narrow medieval streets. Friday-Saturday most lively.

items.label: Drink agua de Valencia
items.sub: Fresh orange juice and cava. Café Madrid is the original venue. Order by the jug — it should be fresh, not concentrate.

items.label: Eat seafood in El Cabanyal
items.sub: Former fishing neighbourhood near the beach. Casa Montaña since 1836. Clóchinas (Valencia mussels). €3-5 per plate.

items.label: Go to Albufera Lake
items.sub: 20km from the city, 40 minutes by bus. El Palmar village, wooden boat tour. Sunset is spectacular. Birthplace of paella.

items.label: Explore City of Arts and Sciences
items.sub: Calatrava's futuristic structures. Walking around outside is free; inside is ticketed. Least crowded in the early morning hours.

checklist.title: Valencia Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Valencia has quietly got under your skin — you know you'll be back without quite knowing when.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Valencia is an easy-going city; its traps are few — but on paella it is merciless. Know these four and speak the city's language.

items.name: 'Paella mixta' on a dinner menu
items.description: Chicken-and-prawn 'mixta' is a tourist invention, and dinner paella is usually lunch's leftovers; a Valencian smiles at both and sits at neither.
items.instead: Order paella at lunch, at an arrocería, for two or more; wood-fired seaside classics like Casa Carmela are a masterclass of their own.

items.name: Doorway inviters on the beach promenade
items.description: The menu-waving restaurants along Malvarrosa sell the day's tired pan to tourists.
items.instead: One street inland, into El Cabanyal's azulejo-fronted lanes: century-old bodegas like Casa Montaña serve tapas and history together.

items.name: The 'all-inclusive' rush at the City of Arts
items.description: Ticketing every building in one day is expensive and exhausting; half the complex is at its best from outside anyway.
items.instead: Pick one building (the Oceanogràfic is the fullest) and live the rest as architecture on foot — at sunset the concrete and water mirror are a free show.

items.name: A jug of 'Agua de Valencia' at a tourist bar
items.description: The city's cocktail is sold everywhere, but in most places it's a version watered down with cheap fizz.
items.instead: Drink it near where it was born: at long-standing bars like Café de las Horas, with cava and fresh orange — one jug serves two, believe it.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Keep Valencia's mealtimes: paella at 2 pm, horchata mid-afternoon, dinner at 9. Match the city's clock and you win the city's kitchen.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the market to the future, along the riverbed

steps.title: Mercado Central
steps.description: Breakfast in one of Europe's most beautiful covered markets: fresh fruit, jamón, an espresso. Across the street, the Gothic pillars of the Silk Exchange.

steps.title: The lanes of El Carmen
steps.description: From medieval gates to street art: climb the Torres de Serranos and look down on the city.

steps.title: Paella — the real one
steps.description: Paella valenciana at an arrocería at lunchtime: rabbit, chicken, garrofón. Spoon fights over the socarrat crust are permitted.

steps.title: Cycling the Turia gardens
steps.description: The dried riverbed is a 9-km green ribbon; glide by pedal to the City of Arts and Sciences.

steps.title: Golden hour at the City of Arts
steps.description: Calatrava's white structures strike the water mirror at sunset; the city's best photo comes from here.

steps.title: Ruzafa evening
steps.description: Tapas + agua de Valencia in the city's liveliest quarter; the night finds its own rhythm here.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Centre and future
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: market, El Carmen, paella, Calatrava.

steps.title: Sea and Cabanyal
steps.description: The sea at Malvarrosa in the morning, Cabanyal's azulejo lanes and Casa Montaña at noon, farm-fresh horchata in Alboraya mid-afternoon, a beachside evening to close.

steps.title: Albufera and goodbye
steps.description: An afternoon boat on the Albufera lake, sunset among the rice paddies — the landscape where paella was born; all i pebre in El Palmar on the way back.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Spanish does the job; a pinch of Valencian wins the heart.

items.meaning: Good morning in Valencian — guaranteed smiles at the neighbourhood bakery
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — agua de Valencia glasses rise to this
Valencian slang for 'mate' — hear che nano! and you're a local now
